title.en: O(1) Lookups: Why Sets Crush Lists for Membership

description.en: Checking `x in a_list` scans every element — O(n). `x in a_set` is near-instant — O(1). One data-structure swap can turn a sluggish loop into a fast one. Feel the difference.

story_variants.en:
## The Cheapest Speedup in Python

"You have 10,000 known-bad IDs and a million requests to check against them," Vaathiyaar says. "Store the bad IDs in a **list** and every check scans up to 10,000 items — billions of comparisons. Store them in a **set** and each check is a single hash lookup. Same code shape, thousands of times faster. This is the cheapest performance win there is."

### Why the Difference

- `x in some_list` — Python walks the list element by element: **O(n)**.
- `x in some_set` (or dict key) — Python hashes `x` and jumps straight to its bucket: **O(1)** on average.

So when you repeatedly test membership, convert your collection to a `set` **once**, then check against it:

```
bad = set(bad_ids)            # one-time cost
[r for r in requests if r in bad]   # each check is O(1)
```

The rule generalizes: lists are for order and iteration; sets and dicts are for fast lookup and de-duplication.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** if you see `in a_list` inside a loop, you've found a speedup. Hoist the collection into a set once, and every check gets cheap.

Today you implement `count_flagged(items, flagged)` — how many `items` appear in `flagged`, using a set for fast membership.

explanation.en: Pay the O(n) conversion cost ONCE
